headlines.summary: Starshield is SpaceX's military-grade satellite network designed for government and national security use, building on the technology developed for Starlink.
headlines.article_text: Ukraine says SpaceX’s Starshield faces speed restrictions Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that fresh restrictions on Starshield operations over Ukraine had been imposed. He said Ukraine is trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side. Similar speed limitations were imposed last month at speeds above 160 kilometers per hour. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was investigating what he described as fresh restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield service over the country, after similar speed limitations were temporarily imposed last month. "Our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now – along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he wrote on X early Thursday. Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network for government and national-security use, built on Starlink technology. CNBC has reached out to SpaceX and the White House for comment. What to know about Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused Starlink service "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he said, adding that they are trying to establish the circumstances with the U.S. Zelenskyy said the restrictions imposed an effective speed limit on terminals moving at speeds above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), disconnecting anything that was moving faster and making it harder for Ukraine to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. "There have already been strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time." On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by cutting connectivity speeds and thereby disrupting military operations. On October 24, Zelenskyy confirmed that systems had returned to their previous operating speeds. According to The Wall Street Journal, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered those restrictions, rendering some Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones virtually unusable. The newspaper later reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had asked Musk to reverse the move. Trump has denied that the White House ordered Starlink restrictions in Ukraine. Musk initially appeared to pin responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government, writing on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." He later claimed Ukraine had violated Starlink's terms of service, prompting the company to restrict its access to the high-speed satellite technology, something that Ukrainian officials have strongly contested . Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense tech advisor to Zelenskyy, said at the time that Ukraine cannot use commercial Starlink for medium- or long-range drone strikes because the service does not operate over Russian territory and had imposed drone speed limits of 70–90 kilometers per hour for months. On Thursday, Beskrestnov confirmed that "the speed of Starlink operation during movement was again limited." "We did not rejoice for long," he said, adding that "any terms can be changed and discussed, instead of leaving our country without sky protection." Peace talks The comments came as U.S.-brokered peace talks wrapped up in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday and U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow for further talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin . Witkoff and Kushner were met by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev as they arrived at Vnukovo Airport on Thursday morning, according to Russian state news agency Tass. The pair were expected to discuss a lasting resolution to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has now raged for more than four-and-a-half years. Later on Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner are poised to meet with Zelenskyy on the sidelines of a political summit held in Ireland. Trilateral talks in the United Arab Emirates between Ukrainian, Russian and American negotiators ended earlier this week without a major diplomatic breakthrough on a ceasefire or territorial settlement. Lutnick should ban Chinese memory maker CXMT from U.S., Sen. Cotton says
headlines.summary: Sen. Tom Cotton is urging the Commerce secretary to add CXMT to its "Entity List" as the fast-growing Chinese memory maker expands in DRAM and pushes into HBM.
headlines.article_text: Lutnick should ban Chinese memory maker CXMT from U.S., Cotton says Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Sen. Tom Cotton is urging the Commerce Department to add Chinese memory maker CXMT to its "Entity List," which would sharply restrict its access to U.S. technology. Cotton, in a letter obtained first by CNBC, warned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against allowing the company to grow its global footprint. The company is challenging memory heavyweights Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix—and pushing into HBM, the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, conducts a news conference in the U.S. Capitol after the Senate Republican leadership elections, Nov. 10, 2026. Tom Williams | CQ-Roll Call, Inc. | Getty Images Sen. Tom Cotton , R-Ark., is urging the Trump administration to take a harsher stance towards Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies . "CXMT, one of Communist China's national memory chip champions, poses a growing risk to our economic prosperity and military superiority," Cotton wrote in a letter sent Thursday to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. "The U.S. must take action to prevent CXMT from gaining a stronger foothold in the global market." CXMT is the world's fourth-largest producer of DRAM – or dynamic random access memory – which powers many basic functions of computers and smartphones. Cotton, in a letter first obtained by CNBC, is asking Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to push CXMT onto the department's Bureau of Industry and Security Entity List, which would significantly restrict U.S. firms' ability to do business with the company. "It basically means that U.S. companies are not allowed to do business with that entity-listed company, and that entity-listed company does not get access to U.S. technology," said Kyle Chan, a Brookings Institution fellow who studies China's technology development. DRAM is a "commodity," Counterpoint research director MS Hwang told CNBC, meaning it is made to a global standard and is generally interchangeable from one manufacturer to another. However, with the right production technology, it can also form the building blocks of HBM, or high-bandwidth memory. HBM is an extremely high-demand product that powers AI chips made by Nvidia , Google and Amazon Web Services, which are central to the growth of artificial intelligence giants including Anthropic and OpenAI. It's made by just three main companies: Samsung , SK Hynix and Micron . A general view shows facilities related to Changxin Memory Technologies, Sept. 4, 2026 in Qingdao, Shandong Province of China. VCG | Visual China Group | Getty Images Those same three companies control the lion's share of the DRAM market, but CXMT has made inroads. The company's share of the DRAM market jumped from just 4% to 10% by revenue in just a year, from the second quarter of 2025 to the same quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint using the most recent reporting available. And in July, the company went public and its stock price soared, making it the most valuable company listed in China at the time . While the company's HBM capabilities are nascent, according to Counterpoint, Reuters reported that the company was to begin production of the chips, even though yields are low at just 20% to 30%. That means that the majority of the chips it produces are faulty.tit CXMT is already on the Pentagon's "1260H" list , which identifies several dozen Chinese companies with ties to Beijing's military. But Chan says that list doesn't come with stringent restrictions for U.S. businesses. "It's not a list that has that much teeth to it, in terms of restrictions to US companies working with Chinese firms on that list," Chan said. The Wall Street Journal reported Aug. 9 that Apple was considering using CXMT's memory in iPhones and Macs in light of the global shortage driven by the AI buildout. Being on the Entity List could change that. "From the U.S. government standpoint, their concern is that working with CXMT would – even as a customer, just buying their products – would help to improve their ability to ramp up memory chip production, and also maybe help China get further down the road towards HBM," Chan said. "It's part of the broader effort to stymie or slow down China's own chip development." Cotton alluded to CXMT's efforts to break into the HBM market in his letter. "[CXMT's] decision to move forward in less than ideal conditions highlights both Communist China's desperation for chips and manufacturing struggles without advanced equipment and knowledge," he wrote. "More can be done to ensure that CXMT is cut off from the financial and technological resources that aid its supply chain and undercut American growth."
